title: Java Syntax Essentials & Clean Coding Standards

activities.title: The Pillars of Java Syntax & Code Style
activities.content:
### The 4 Non-Negotiable Syntax Rules

#### 1. Strict Case Sensitivity
Java treats uppercase and lowercase letters as completely different characters. 
* `System` (uppercase S) is a valid Java standard class.
* `system` (lowercase s) will trigger `error: cannot find symbol`.
* Variables `totalMarks`, `TotalMarks`, and `TOTALMARKS` are three completely unrelated variables in Java.

#### 2. Every Statement Ends With a Semicolon (`;`)
A semicolon signals to the Java compiler that an instruction is complete. Unlike Python or JavaScript, semicolons are mandatory in Java. Forgetting a semicolon triggers the famous `error: ';' expected`.
* Note: Structural blocks like `class Main { ... }` and `public static void main(...) { ... }` do NOT end with a semicolon; they are enclosed in curly braces.

#### 3. Matching Curly Braces (`{` and `}`)
Curly braces define a **code block** (a scope). Every opening brace `{` must have a matching closing brace `}`. In modern software engineering, you always indent code inside braces by 4 spaces for readability.

#### 4. Industry Naming Conventions
While the compiler allows strange names, professional engineering teams follow standard naming conventions:
* **Classes**: Use **PascalCase** (UpperCamelCase). Every word starts with a capital letter.
  * Examples: `Main`, `StudentRecord`, `PaymentGatewayService`.
* **Variables & Methods**: Use **camelCase**. Starts with a lowercase letter, subsequent words capitalized.
  * Examples: `studentAge`, `totalAmount`, `calculateInterestRate()`.
* **Constants**: Use **ALL_CAPS_WITH_UNDERSCORES**.
  * Examples: `MAX_RETRIES`, `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT`.

### Writing Clean Comments
Comments are notes written for humans reading the code:
* Single-line comments start with `//`.
* Multi-line comments are enclosed between `/*` and `*/`.
* **Important Fact**: The Java compiler completely strips out all comments during compilation. They do not appear in the `.class` bytecode and have zero effect on program speed or file size.

breakdown.whatIsIt: Java syntax is the set of grammar rules governing how programs are written, punctuated, and structured.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Writing syntactically clean code eliminates compiler failures and ensures your code passes automated coding round evaluations.
howItWorks: 1. Match every opening brace with a closing brace
2. Terminate every statement with a semicolon (;)
3. Follow PascalCase for classes and camelCase for methods and variables
keyTakeaways: Java is strictly case-sensitive: System != system
Classes use PascalCase (Main, OrderService); variables use camelCase (orderTotal)
Comments (// and /* */) are stripped during compilation and carry zero runtime cost

activities.title: A Cleanly Formatted, Documented Java Program
activities.description: Notice clean camelCase for variables (`accountHolder`, `accountBalance`), PascalCase for the class (`Main`), and purposeful single-line and multi-line comments explaining context.

questions.question: Which of the following class names follows the standard Java naming convention?
questions.explanation: Java classes use PascalCase (UpperCamelCase), where each word starts with a capital letter (StudentRecord).
hints: Classes start with an uppercase letter and capitalize subsequent words.

questions.question: What happens when you compile Java code that contains extensive multi-line comments?
options: The comments increase the size of the compiled .class file.
The comments are completely removed by the compiler and have zero effect on bytecode or performance.
The JVM reads the comments during runtime to optimize execution.
The compiler fails if comments exceed 100 lines.
questions.explanation: The Java compiler (javac) discards all comments during the lexical analysis phase. The generated .class bytecode contains zero comment text.
hints: Comments are strictly for human readers; the computer has no use for them.

questions.question: Which line of code will cause a compilation error due to case sensitivity?
questions.explanation: system.out.println with a lowercase 's' fails because the class name is 'System'. Java is strictly case-sensitive.
hints: Look for the lowercase 's' on the built-in System class.

practice.title: Assignment: Format a Clean Inventory Receipt
practice.problemStatement:
Write a complete Java program in the Main class that prints a formatted inventory report with exactly 3 lines:

Item: Mechanical Keyboard
Category: Computer Peripherals
In Stock: Yes
requirements: Include a single-line comment above the main method
Print exactly the 3 required lines using System.out.println
practice.expectedOutput:
Item: Mechanical Keyboard
Category: Computer Peripherals
In Stock: Yes
hints: Check spelling of 'Mechanical Keyboard' and 'Computer Peripherals'.
Make sure each println call ends with a semicolon (;).

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between syntax errors and logical errors?
interviewQA.answer: A syntax error violates the grammatical rules of Java (e.g., missing semicolon, unmatched brace, misspelled keyword) and prevents the compiler (javac) from generating a .class file. A logical error occurs when code compiles and runs cleanly, but produces an incorrect or unintended result due to flawed algorithm logic (e.g., subtracting numbers when you meant to add).
interviewQA.keyTakeaway: Syntax errors are caught at compile time by javac; logical errors can only be caught through testing.

interviewQA.question: Why does Java enforce camelCase for variables and PascalCase for classes?
interviewQA.answer: While the compiler does not reject lowercase class names (it will compile `class student`), following standard Java conventions is vital for readability and maintainability. When an engineer sees `StudentRecord`, they instantly know it is a class or type; when they see `studentRecord`, they know it is a variable or object instance. This distinction prevents ambiguity in large enterprise codebases.
interviewQA.keyTakeaway: Conventions make code instantly understandable across large development teams.
